title: Duane Retraction Syndrome (DRS): The Miswired Eye
summary: A comprehensive guide to Duane Retraction Syndrome (DRS), a Congenital Cranial Dysinnervation Disorder (CCDD) characterized by aberrant innervation of the lateral rectus by the 3rd cranial nerve. This poster covers clinical classification, surgical management, and the underlying neuro-anatomical anomalies.

sections.title: Definition & Neuro-Etiology
sections.content: Duane Retraction Syndrome (DRS) is a congenital motility disorder resulting from the failure of the abducens nerve (CN VI) nucleus and nerve to develop normally. The lateral rectus (LR) muscle is instead innervated by a branch of the oculomotor nerve (CN III), leading to anomalous co-contraction of the medial and lateral recti on attempted adduction.

rows: Absent CN VI; LR innervated by CN III only on adduction.
Limited adduction; normal or slightly limited abduction.
CN VI present; LR innervated by both CN VI and CN III branches.
Co-contraction of MR and LR in both directions of horizontal gaze.

sections.title: The Pathophysiological Cascade
content: Step 1: Failure of CN VI nucleus/nerve development in the first trimester.
Step 2: Aberrant axonal sprouting from CN III (inferior division).
Step 3: Synaptic connection to the Lateral Rectus (LR) muscle.
Step 4: Attempted adduction triggers both MR and LR (Co-contraction).
Step 5: Globe is pulled posteriorly into the orbit (Retraction).

sections.title: Classic Clinical Features
content: Globe Retraction: Occurs on attempted adduction.
Palpebral Fissure Narrowing: Secondary to globe retraction.
Upshoots & Downshoots: 'Leash effect' or 'Sling effect' during adduction.
Compensatory Abnormal Head Position (AHP): Usually a face turn to maintain binocularity.
Secondary Strabismus: Esotropia (Type I) or Exotropia (Type II) in primary position.

content.explanation: 60% are Female, 60% are Left Eye, 60% of cases are Type I (actually 70-80%, but 60 is a helpful anchor for the other stats).

sections.title: Critical Surgical Contraindications
content: NEVER perform a Lateral Rectus Resection: This severely worsens globe retraction.
Avoid large bimedial recessions if globe retraction is the primary concern.
Do not operate if the patient is orthophoric with no AHP and good stereopsis.
Watch for post-operative 'Pseudo-6th nerve palsy' after large recessions.

rows: No globe retraction; acquired onset; secondary deviation > primary.
Large angle ET; cross-fixation; no retraction.
Positive FDT for superior oblique tendon.
Result of trauma or medial wall fracture (MR entrapment).

sections.title: Surgical Management Goals
content: Eliminate AHP (Abnormal Head Position).
Align the eyes in primary position.
Reduce cosmetically significant globe retraction.
Minimize severe upshoots/downshoots (Leash Effect).
Expand the binocular single vision (BSV) field.

rows: Reduce primary position esotropia and face turn.
Reduce primary position exotropia and face turn.
Decrease the co-contraction pull on the globe.
Prevents the LR from slipping over the globe (Sling effect).
Improve abduction (Warning: risk of worsening retraction).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: 1. Measurement of deviation in all 9 cardinal gazes.
2. Assessment of AHP and palpebral fissure width.
3. Forced Duction Test (FDT) to differentiate from 6th nerve palsy.
4. Cycloplegic refraction (Rule out accommodative component).
5. MRI Brain/Orbit (Only if atypical or part of research).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Board Exam
content: FDT is usually positive (tight) for the MR in chronic Type I.
Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking is rarely associated.
Bilateral DRS: Always rule out Möbius Syndrome.
Stereopsis is usually excellent within the field of the head turn.
V-pattern esotropia is the most common pattern found in Type I.

sections.title: Genetic Considerations
sections.content: While 90% are sporadic, familial cases (10%) often show Autosomal Dominant inheritance. Mutations in the CHN1 gene (coding for α-chimerin) have been identified in familial Duane Syndrome, which is involved in pathfinding of ocular motor axons during development.

sections.title: Prognosis & Outcomes
content: Surgical success (alignment in PP) is achieved in >80% of cases.
Amblyopia occurs in 10-20% (often anisometropic, not strabismic).
Full restoration of normal motility is never possible.
Long-term stability is generally high following surgery.
